newsitem.title: USA: NYS seeking one-year waiver for Food Stamps.
newsitem.headline: NYS seeking one-year waiver for Food Stamps.

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki, who fought asking Washington for a broad waiver from new work rules for Food Stamps recipients, wants a one-year exemption where jobs are scarce, a state official said Friday.

A spokesman for the state Department of Social Services, Terence McGrath, said that the Pataki Administration would ask the Department of Agriculture, which runs the federally funded Food Stamps program, for a one-year waiver. He had no further details immediately available.

Rus Sykes, deputy director of the State Community Aid Association, an advocacy group for the poor, said the state would ask the federal government to waive the new workfare rules for Food Stamps from November 1996 to November 1997.

"It'll be a broad waiver for all localities that meet labor surplus criteria," he said, explaining that this means that those counties that can prove, using labor data, that there are too many people looking for too few jobs, will not have to apply the rules during that period. "This will exempt all of New York City, a host of other counties, and in some cases, portions of counties," Sykes said.

The Pataki Administration last year requested a much narrower exemption, which only would have waived the new work rules in areas where the unemployment rate exceeds 10 percent. The work requirements oblige single, able-bodied adults from 18 years old to 50 years old to work at least 20 hours a week in order to collect Food Stamps.

The New York Times on Friday said that the only areas in New York where unemployment exceeded 10 percent were the Bronx and Hamilton County, in the southern Adirondacks. The issue of the state's levels of unemployment is a sensitive one for the Pataki Administration, which has promoted its ability to create new jobs.
A spokeswoman for the state Department of Labor referred calls to the Division of Budget, whose spokesman was not immediately available to comment.
Sykes explained that the waiver would be retroactive in order to meet the requirements of the new federal rules, which would have begun March 1, after a three-month notice period.

Pataki, a Republican, has proposed a new welform program, needed to put the state in compliance with the new federal laws though the governor's plan is tougher in some areas. The Assembly, which is controlled by Democrats, rejected Pataki's previous efforts to change the state's welfare system, and Sykes said that by mid-March it likely would come up with an alternative plan or recommend changes to Pataki's proposals.

While the Assembly's new plan is expected to stay within the bounds of the new federal rules, which became law last August, Sykes suggested it might seek to temper some of Pataki's program by giving cash assistance to single adults and extending the temporary disability program, for example.

Under Pataki's plan, the state's Home Relief program, which aids able-bodies adults who do not have children, would be replaced with Safety Net plan that would give them vouchers to help them get food, clothing and shelter.
A spokesman for Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, was not immediately available to comment.
